assumptions: Assumes the service stores or further processes uploaded videos and moderation outcomes.

title: Lack of adequate evidence about upload submission and approval/rejection decisions may undermine accountability to the parent user
description: If the service does not maintain privacy-respecting records of what was uploaded, when consent or submission occurred, and why a video was approved or rejected, the parent user may be unable to demonstrate or challenge the handling of their personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the workflow includes decisions affecting the user's content and rights.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; retrieved context did not provide the detailed Non-repudiation subtree.

title: Video stream can enable linkage of the child across sessions or contexts
description: Delivering an approved video stream to the child may expose persistent identifiers or stable metadata in the stream delivery path, allowing the child device, network observers, or third-party delivery components to link multiple viewing sessions or correlate the child with other activity.
assumptions: Assumes the stream or associated delivery mechanism carries stable identifiers such as account IDs, device IDs, session tokens reused across sessions, or uniquely identifying URLs.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context confirms L applies to Process→ExternalEntity flows but did not provide a more specific linkage subtree citation.

title: Video delivery may reveal identifying information about the child or account
description: The outbound stream may contain direct or indirect identifiers in headers, URLs, captions, watermarking, personalization metadata, or embedded analytics parameters that identify the child, household, or account to recipients or intermediaries.
assumptions: Assumes personalized streaming, CDN delivery, analytics beacons, or watermarking are used.
uncertainty_note: Specific subtree node is selected by best judgement because the retrieved context only established applicability of Identifiability to this flow type.

title: Streaming content consumption may disclose the child's viewing behavior
description: Sending the approved video to the child inherently reveals that this child account or device is watching specific content at a specific time. This can disclose preferences, habits, routines, age-related inferences, or other personal aspects if observed by service operators, delivery partners, or network intermediaries.
assumptions: Assumes viewing events are observable through delivery logs, CDN access records, or network metadata.
uncertainty_note: Threat is grounded in the privacy disclosure caused by the flow itself; exact D subtree node is chosen by best judgement.

title: The child may be unaware of personal-data disclosure inherent in streaming
description: The child user may not be aware that requesting and receiving a video stream discloses personal data such as viewing history, timestamps, IP address, device characteristics, and engagement information to the service and possibly third-party delivery providers.
assumptions: Assumes notices are absent, unclear, or not understandable for a child audience.
uncertainty_note: Applicability is plausible for child-facing streaming, but evidence about actual notice design is not provided.

title: Streaming may be used for purposes unexpected by the child
description: Data generated by delivering the approved video may be processed beyond the child's reasonable expectations, such as profiling engagement, personalization, recommendation tuning, advertising measurement, or sharing with content-delivery and analytics providers.
assumptions: Assumes secondary use of streaming telemetry or delivery metadata beyond the core purpose of showing the approved video.
uncertainty_note: Exact secondary uses are not stated in the flow description, so this is contingent on common streaming-service practices.

title: Streaming approved video to a child may violate child-data handling obligations
description: Delivering the stream may involve processing children's personal data, including viewing history and device/network metadata. If the service lacks an appropriate legal basis, age-appropriate transparency, data minimization, retention limits, or controls on third-party sharing, this flow can create non-compliance with child-privacy and personal-data management obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the child is a protected minor under applicable law and that streaming generates or shares personal data.
uncertainty_note: Nc.2 is directly supported by retrieved context, but the actual compliance posture of the system is not provided.

title: Excessive disclosure of child browsing data to the AI recommendation engine
description: The planned flow sends child browsing data from the childprofiles collection to the AI recommendation engine. If the full browsing history or overly granular events are transferred when only aggregated or limited features are needed for recommendations, the flow discloses more personal data than necessary for the stated purpose. Because the data concerns children, the privacy impact is heightened.
assumptions: Assumes the recommendation engine does not strictly require the full raw browsing dataset and could operate on minimized, filtered, or aggregated inputs.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best judgement for a data-minimization/avoidable disclosure case; exact node label may vary across LINDDUN Pro versions.

title: Secondary use of child browsing data for AI-driven profiling beyond user expectations
description: Using stored child browsing data as input to an AI recommendation engine may be incompatible with the original context in which the data was collected, especially if users or guardians would reasonably expect storage for account or service operation but not model-driven profiling or personalization. This creates a risk that the processing purpose is unclear, expanded, or not sufficiently aligned with expectations.
assumptions: Assumes the planned AI recommendation purpose was not clearly specified and communicated at collection time, or is materially different from the original purpose for storing the browsing data.
uncertainty_note: Exact applicability depends on the stated original purpose and notices/consent presented to guardians; tree node is best-effort.

title: Processing child browsing data for recommendations without a clear lawful basis or age-appropriate consent
description: The planned transfer enables AI processing of children's browsing data, which may require explicit parental authorization, age-appropriate transparency, and purpose-specific consent or another valid lawful basis depending on jurisdiction. If those conditions are absent or insufficiently documented, the flow creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the dataset contains personal data about children and that the recommendation use case may be subject to stricter children's privacy and consent requirements.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations are jurisdiction-dependent; node chosen as a generic non-compliance/invalid legal basis case.

title: Inference of sensitive traits or preferences from child browsing data by the AI engine
description: Even if the input data does not explicitly contain sensitive attributes, an AI recommendation engine can infer interests, habits, vulnerabilities, developmental characteristics, or potentially sensitive categories from browsing patterns. The flow therefore enables additional privacy-invasive knowledge to be derived from the transferred data.
assumptions: Assumes the recommendation engine performs profiling or feature extraction on browsing behavior rather than simple rule-based matching.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is selected by best judgement for inference from behavioral data; exact node numbering may differ by catalog version.

title: Excessive disclosure of browsing data to third-party advertisers
description: The planned flow intentionally shares users' browsing data from the AI Recommendation Engine to third-party advertisers. This is a cross-boundary transfer of personal data and may disclose more data than is strictly necessary for any legitimate advertising purpose, violating data minimization and creating avoidable exposure to third parties.
assumptions: Browsing data is personal data or can reasonably be linked to an identifiable user or profile; advertisers are outside the system boundary and act as third parties.

title: Browsing-data sharing enables identification by advertisers
description: Even if the shared browsing data is not intended to directly identify users, advertisers may combine it with existing identifiers, cookies, device fingerprints, or account data to identify or single out individuals. The outgoing flow therefore creates a realistic identifiability threat.
assumptions: Third-party advertisers possess auxiliary datasets or tracking identifiers that can be linked with the browsing data.
uncertainty_note: Exact I subtree node is best-judgement; retrieved context establishes that Identifiability applies to Process→ExternalEntity flows, but not the precise node id.

title: Cross-context linkage of browsing behavior across services
description: Sharing browsing data with third-party advertisers can allow those advertisers to link a user's behavior in this system with behavior observed on other sites, apps, or datasets. This enables construction of broader cross-service profiles beyond the original context of collection.
assumptions: Advertisers can correlate the received data with their own identifiers or partner data.
uncertainty_note: Exact L subtree node is best-judgement; linkage is strongly plausible for advertiser data-sharing, but the retrieved context does not provide the specific node id.

title: Sharing browsing data may reveal sensitive interests or habits
description: Browsing data often exposes interests, routines, preferences, and potentially special-category inferences such as health, politics, religion, sexuality, or financial concerns. Sending this data to advertisers can therefore make users detectable or observable with respect to sensitive traits or behaviors.
assumptions: Browsing histories or events contain URLs, categories, timestamps, or recommendation interactions from which sensitive interests can be inferred.

title: Planned advertiser sharing may be incompatible with user consent or purpose limitation

This creates a non-compliance risk regarding lawful basis, transparency, purpose limitation, and data minimization.

title: Excessive retention or storage of government ID images
description: Government ID images are highly sensitive personal data. Storing full images in backend/uploads/ may disclose more personal data than is strictly necessary for authentication or verification purposes, especially if the entire image is retained rather than extracting only required attributes or storing a less sensitive verification result.
assumptions: Assumes the service stores full ID images and may retain them beyond the minimum period or scope needed for identity verification.

title: Stored ID images enable identification of the data subject
description: A government ID image directly contains strong identifiers such as name, photograph, document number, date of birth, and sometimes address. Persisting these images in the file system makes the data store capable of directly identifying individuals.
assumptions: Assumes uploaded images are readable originals or scans of official identity documents.
uncertainty_note: Identification is inherent to government ID images; exact subtree id is best-effort because no detailed I subtree was provided in the retrieved context.

title: Storage of government ID images may exceed necessity or legal basis
description: Persisting government ID images in a backend file store may be unnecessary or disproportionate if the purpose can be achieved with less data, temporary inspection, extracted attributes, or a tokenized verification result. This creates a non-compliance risk with data minimization, storage limitation, and purpose limitation principles.
assumptions: Assumes no demonstrated requirement exists to retain full ID images after verification.
uncertainty_note: Exact Nc subtree id is best-effort; applicability is grounded in common privacy-law principles rather than a retrieved subtree citation.

title: JWT in localStorage enables cross-context linkability
description: Persisting a JWT in browser localStorage creates a stable client-side identifier/token that can be reused across sessions and application contexts on the same origin. If multiple pages, scripts, or components access the same token, user actions can be linked together over time.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT contains a stable subject/session identifier and remains accessible to same-origin scripts until cleared or expired.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicable threat types for Process->DataStore, not the detailed LINDDUN Pro subtree for linkability.

title: JWT contents may identify the user
description: A JWT stored in localStorage may contain directly or indirectly identifying claims such as subject, email, username, tenant, roles, or other unique attributes. Any same-origin script able to read localStorage can identify the user from the token contents or by presenting the token to backend services.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT is not strongly minimized and contains user-related claims, or can be exchanged for identity information by the application.
uncertainty_note: Exact JWT claim set is not provided; if the token is opaque or contains no identifying claims, identifiability would be reduced though backend use of the token may still identify the user.

title: localStorage persistence increases detectability of user presence
description: Because localStorage persists across browser restarts and sessions, same-origin code can detect whether a JWT is present and infer that a user has previously authenticated or is currently returning. This reveals the existence of an account/session even before explicit user interaction.
assumptions: Assumes scripts on the origin can check for token presence and that token lifetime exceeds a single page load.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; retrieved context does not include detailed detectability subtree nodes.

title: JWT storage in localStorage exposes sensitive authentication data to scripts
description: Storing a JWT in localStorage makes the token readable by any JavaScript executing in the origin, including injected or third-party scripts. This can disclose authentication and embedded personal data beyond what is necessary, enabling token theft and privacy compromise.
assumptions: Assumes browser-side scripts can access localStorage and that the JWT itself or its use reveals personal/session information.
uncertainty_note: Although disclosure here is strongly supported by common web security/privacy practice, the exact LINDDUN Pro subtree id is chosen by best judgement due to missing detailed node list in context.

title: Persistent JWT storage may exceed user expectations or consent
description: Persisting an authentication token in localStorage can retain personal/session data longer than users expect, especially if they believe closing the browser ends the session. If retention period, purpose, or access by scripts is not transparently communicated and controlled, storage may violate consent and data-minimization expectations.
assumptions: Assumes the application does not clearly inform users about persistent token storage, retention, and logout/clearing behavior.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on jurisdiction, notices, and implemented controls; this is a plausible privacy threat rather than a certain legal violation.

If the returned history includes stable identifiers, timestamps, locations, device data, or cross-context activity details, the parent can link separate events into a richer profile of the child than is necessary for the immediate review purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the history payload contains multiple records and recurring identifiers or quasi-identifiers enabling correlation across time or contexts.

description: If the interface does not clearly explain what child-history data is included, from which sources it was collected, over what retention period, and why it is shown, the child and parent may lack awareness of the processing behind this disclosure. This undermines transparency for the data subject whose history is being reviewed.

The flow enables such use if purpose limitation is not enforced or communicated.

description: Providing child history to the parent may violate consent arrangements, age-dependent privacy rights, custody restrictions, or internal policy if the system does not verify that this parent is entitled to receive each category of history data. The privacy threat arises from non-compliant disclosure through this flow.
assumptions: Assumes entitlement to review child history can vary by jurisdiction, child age, custody status, or data category.
